intro:
**The Manifest Triumph and the Sanctuary of Tranquility**

Al-Fatḥ, "The Triumph" or "The Victory," is the forty-eighth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 29 verses of late Medinan revelation. It takes its name from its electrifying opening proclamation: *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph (*fatḥan mubīnā*)”* (48:1). In prophetic tradition, Sūrah al-Fatḥ holds an exalted, emotionally overwhelming station: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4833) that while riding with the Prophet ﷺ on the return journey from Ḥudaybiyah, the Messenger of Allah turned to him and declared: *“Tonight, a chapter has been revealed to me that is dearer to me than the entire world and everything within it!”*—and then recited the opening of Sūrah al-Fatḥ. Uniquely, the "clear triumph" celebrated in this chapter was not a military slaughter or the physical conquest of a citadel; it was the historic Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah in 6 AH—a peace pact that appeared to human eyes as a bitter diplomatic compromise, yet was recognized by Divine Wisdom as the greatest strategic and spiritual victory in early Islamic history.

**The Structural Modulation and the Garden of the Companions**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Fatḥ moves from divine forgiveness to psychological tranquility, and from battlefield covenants to the glorious biblical portrait of the Companions. The opening movement (1–10) announces total divine forgiveness for the Prophet's past and future liabilities, the completion of divine favor, and the sending down of *al-Sakīnah* (Divine Tranquility) into the hearts of the believers to increase them in faith upon faith. It affirms that the angelic and cosmic hosts of the heavens and earth belong exclusively to Allah, condemns the hypocrites and polytheists who harbored evil suspicions of God, and defines the cosmic weight of the Pledge of the Tree in verse 10: *“Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, [O Muḥammad]—they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. The Hand of Allah is over their hands.”* The second movement (11–17) exposes the cowardice of the bedouin tribes who stayed behind from the expedition, concocting transparent excuses about their wealth and families, and clarifies the legitimate exemptions for the blind, the lame, and the ill. The third movement (18–26) records God's eternal pleasure with the 1,400 believers who took the oath: *“Certainly was Allah pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquility upon them and rewarded them with an imminent conquest”* (48:18). It reveals why God restrained the Muslims' hands from fighting inside Makkah: to protect vulnerable, hidden believing men and women living unknown among the pagans, whom the Muslim army might have trampled unknowingly. The climactic movement (27–29) validates the Prophet's original vision of entering the Sacred Mosque with shaved heads and shortened hair in total security, declaring that Islam has been sent with guidance and the religion of truth to prevail over all religion. The chapter concludes with the magnificent, immortal portrait of the Companions in verse 29: *“Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah; and those with him are forceful against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration.”* It cites their description in the Torah and their parable in the Gospel: like a seed that puts forth its sprout, strengthens it, thickens, and stands firm upon its stem, delighting the sowers, sealed with the divine promise of forgiveness and an immense reward for those who believe and do good.

verses.1:
> Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺

**A Name for What Was to Come**

The commentators divided on what the word names. Many understand it as a reference to the conquest of Makkah and, by extension, to the Muslim victories that followed, on the ground that a triumph spoken of in the past tense at Ḥudaibiyah cannot be the event at which it was spoken, and must be the event that proves it. Others, and among them Ibn Masʿūd and Anas ibn Mālik, understand it as the treaty itself, because the treaty did what a conquest would have done more slowly: it let the two peoples mix freely, and the mixing produced the spread. The later verse about the fulfilled vision (48:27 — *“Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger’s vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security—˹some with˺ heads shaved and ˹others with˺ hair shortened—without fear. He knew what you did not know, so He first granted you the triumph at hand”*) holds the two together, since the entry it predicts is the same entry the opening was worked for.

**The Companion Who Could Not Accept It**

The verse's claim was not received as news of victory. The most forceful objector at Ḥudaibiyah was ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and he did not merely object; he interrogated. In the account preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (3182), he asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Aren't we in the right and our opponents in the wrong?" He was told, "Yes." He pressed on: were the slain of both sides where he assumed them to be? Yes. "Then why should we accept hard terms in matters about our religion? Shall we return before Allah judges between us and them?" The answer given him was not a proof but a status: "I am the Messenger of Allah. Allah will never degrade me." Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have summarized the community's later view with equal directness, saying that the Quraysh considered the conquest of Makkah to be the victory, while to the companions the victory was the treaty conducted at Ḥudaibiyah. The objection survives in the same traditions as the treaty itself, which tells the reader that the verdict of this verse was not unanimous at the moment it fell.

**A Sentence Left Unfinished**

The grammar of the verse is the smallest piece of evidence for its meaning.

The verse states the triumph and then stops. The purpose behind it does not arrive until the verse that follows, and when it arrives it arrives as a chain: forgiveness (48:2 states it — *“so that Allah may forgive you for your past and future shortcomings, perfect His favour upon you, guide you along the Straight Path”*), help that is tremendous (48:3 states it — *“and so that Allah will help you tremendously”*), serenity sent down into hearts (48:4 states it — *“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith.”*), admission to the gardens (48:5 states it — *“So He may admit believing men and women into Gardens under which rivers flow—to stay there forever—and absolve them of their sins. And that is a supreme achievement in the sight of Allah”*), and the punishment of the people who set themselves against God (48:6 states it — *“Also ˹so that˺ He may punish hypocrite men and women and polytheistic men and women, who harbour evil thoughts of Allah. May ill-fate befall them! Allah is displeased with them. He has condemned them and prepared for them Hell. What an evil destination”*).

The first verse is therefore a subject with a postponed predicate, and the sūrah is the sentence it begins. The device explains a feature that would otherwise be puzzling, namely why the triumph is announced before any of its contents. The reader who knows the end of the story reads the announcement as a receipt: the account of what the opening produced is to follow item by item, and every item that follows can be checked against the claim made here. The sūrah's structure is its first argument, and the argument is that a victory is measured by what it is for, not by the noise it makes.
verses.2:
> so that Allah may forgive you for your past and future shortcomings, perfect His favour upon you, guide you along the Straight Path

**The Feet That Swelled Anyway**

The Prophet's own answer to the verse survives in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (1130, and again in the section on the Prophetic commentary of the Qurʾān, 4836). He stood in night prayer until his feet swelled, and someone told him that Allah had forgiven him his past and future sins — the words of this verse, offered back to him as an answer. His reply was a question: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" The tradition does two things that the exegesis alone could not. It shows the verse functioning in the community's memory as a permission that was declined, and it fixes the Prophet's relation to the verse as gratitude rather than relief. The verse does not say *you may now rest*; it says *your fault is remitted*, and the remission, in the life it is about, produced not an easing of worship but its intensification. Forgiveness here is not the end of the accounting with God; it is what makes the accounting possible without despair, and the swollen feet are the physical proof that the accounting continued.
verses.3:
> and so that Allah will help you tremendously

**The Help That Arrived as Absence**

The help the verse announces arrived in a form the pilgrims did not expect, and the form is the point. At Ḥudaibiyah the help took the shape of what did not happen. The Quraysh, who had barred the camp from the Sacred Mosque and held the envoy, did not attack. The two armies stood facing one another in the valley outside Mecca, and the fighting that the logic of the situation made probable never came. The sūrah will later describe the event in military language: Allah held back their hands from you and your hands from them (48:24 — *“He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them.”*). That holding back is the tremendous help in its material form. A help that is delivered as the absence of catastrophe is hard to recognize at the moment it arrives, because it has no visible agent and no dramatic event, and the community had to have the sūrah to learn what had been done to it. The lesson is structural: the help of God is not always an added force; sometimes it is the removal of the force that was closing in, and the removal is the harder of the two to witness.

**A Later Sūrah Names the Same Help**

The Quran returns to this help in its final and shortest form. The sūrah that names the help of Ḥudaibiyah in the sixth year after the Hijrah is completed by the sūrah an-Nasr, which gives the help its arrival-time: "When Allah's ˹ultimate˺ help comes and the victory ˹over Mecca is achieved˺, and you ˹O Prophet˺ see the people embracing Allah's Way in crowds" (110:1–2). The two sūrahs bracket the same process from its beginning and its end. The help announced at Ḥudaibiyah is the help that arrives at the conquest, and the conquest is the help's visible terminus.

**Forces the Pilgrims Did Not Have**

The sūrah states the help in the next verse in forces, and the contrast is arithmetic. The pilgrims at Ḥudaibiyah numbered in the thousands, carried no siege apparatus, and had come with weapons sheathed to visit, not war; the forces of the heavens and the earth belong, by the sūrah's own statement, to Allah alone (48:4 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth.”*). The tremendous help is, in the sūrah's logic, the help of a force that is not the pilgrims' force, which can act for them without their seeing it act. The Quran gives the precedent: when the Prophet and his companion were in the cave, after the emigration, Allah "supported him with forces you ˹believers˺ did not see" (9:40). The help of this verse belongs to the same class. It is real, it is tremendous, and it is delivered by agents the campaign's participants never counted among their own. The community's later memory of Ḥudaibiyah — as triumph, as the pledge under the tree, as the opening that Mecca could not close — is the record of a help that had arrived while no one was looking for it.
verses.4:
> He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith. To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**What the Sakinah Is**

The verse introduces a word that becomes a technical term in the Quran's own usage: *sakīna*, serenity, the descent of a calm that is not produced by the person who receives it. The sūrah attributes it to Allah's action, "He sent down," and the direction of the verb matters, because the serenity is not something the hearts generate in their own steadiness; it is something that arrives from above, sent, like rain or like the angels. The commentators describe it in several registers, and the registers fit together. It is Allah's mercy made operative in a community under strain. It is an angel, or a presence of angels, settling in the hearts of the believers and steadying them. It is the intellect at its point of balance, the faculty that calms the pull of desire. And it is the state of a person who has been calmed *about* something, the root meaning to settle, to bring to rest, to take the motion out of a thing. What the readings share is the doctrine behind the word: that calm in the face of loss is not a psychological achievement but a gift, and that the gift is addressable, that it can be sent where it is needed.

**Serenity at the Point of Strain**

The sūrah sends the serenity three times in its own text, and the three descents mark the three points of maximum strain. The first is here, at the turning back from the Sacred Mosque. The second is at the pledge under the tree, when the envoy was believed killed and the community was asked to bind itself to a fight it had not come to make (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand”*). The third is at the moment of the pride, when the hearts of the disbelievers had filled with the pride of ignorance and the believers were being tested by the sight of it (48:26 — *“˹Remember˺ when the disbelievers had filled their hearts with pride—the pride of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance—then Allah sent down His serenity upon His Messenger and the believers, inspiring them to uphold the declaration of faith, for they were better entitled and more worthy of it.”*). The Quran gives the precedent of the class: in the cave, at the moment of the most intimate danger of the emigration, Allah "sent down His serenity upon the Prophet, supported him with forces you ˹believers˺ did not see" (9:40). The pattern the sūrah is building is that the serenity arrives at the point of strain, not after it, and that its arrival is the mark of the point. A community's hardest moments are, in this account, the moments at which it is being held, and the sūrah names the holding.
verses.5:
> So He may admit believing men and women into Gardens under which rivers flow—to stay there forever—and absolve them of their sins. And that is a supreme achievement in the sight of Allah

**The Garden Called the Supreme Achievement**

The verse calls the entry into the Gardens a supreme achievement in the sight of Allah, and the phrase is a standing expression in the Quran, used in over a dozen places to mark the highest good that God's decree produces. The usage tells the reader how to read the sūrah's first section as a whole. The triumph announced in the first verse was called *clear*; the Gardens are called a *supreme achievement*, and the two adjectives place the same event at two altitudes. The treaty at Ḥudaibiyah is a clear opening, visible in history; the Gardens are the achievement that the opening was made for, and the sūrah refuses to let the reader stop at the visible altitude.

**Absolution Before Admission**

The order of the two verbs in the verse is part of its meaning. The believers are absolved of their sins, and they are admitted into the Gardens; the absolution comes first, and the admission follows on it. The Quran states the same order elsewhere, most fully in the verse in which God answers the supplicants who asked for forgiveness and for good in both lives: "I will certainly forgive their sins and admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah" (3:195).

---

**The Promise Names Both**

The verse is explicit about who is covered: *that He may admit the believing men and the believing women into gardens under which rivers flow, and remove their misdeeds from them*. The sūrah names men and women together, as it does in the treaties and pledges of this passage, at a time when the weight of public honour in Arabia rested on male participation. The assurance is not addressed to a household's men on behalf of its women; the women are named and promised in their own right.
**Why the Escape Is in the Word**

The phrase rendered *supreme achievement* is *fawz ʿaẓīm*, and *fawz* in Arabic carries the sense of coming out safe — the caravan that reaches its destination with its goods whole. The Book uses the word for the one who is drawn away from the Fire and let into the Garden: whoever is kept from the Fire and entered into Paradise has truly won (3:185 — *“Whoever is spared from the Fire and is admitted into Paradise will ˹indeed˺ triumph, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”*). So the achievement named here is an escape as well as a reward, and the sūrah puts forgiveness next to it. The release of the debt and the entry come together; the verse says the admission was prepared *for them*, and the removal of misdeeds is the way the door is opened.
verses.6:
> Also ˹so that˺ He may punish hypocrite men and women and polytheistic men and women, who harbour evil thoughts of Allah. May ill-fate befall them! Allah is displeased with them. He has condemned them and prepared for them Hell. What an evil destination

**The Thought, Not Only the Deed**

The verse's rarity in the Quran is its object. The Book condemns acts throughout, and the acts of the hostile are elsewhere named in full: the barring of the house, the delay of the envoy, the plotting against the messenger. Here the condemnation is aimed at the heart's calculation, and the reason the thought is named is that it could not be seen. The Quraysh's refusal was visible; the delay of the envoy was visible; the thought that God had been outmanoeuvred was not visible, and it was the one that would produce the next act.

**Why the Verse Closes the First Section**

The verse is the last of the sūrah's first section, and its position is the reason for its completeness. The next verse repeats the sentence about the forces of the heavens and the earth (48:7 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise”*), and the repetition is the section's seal: the same ownership that was stated in the fourth verse is stated again, so that the reader leaves the first section with the ground of the whole account fixed.

---

**The Other Side of the Sentence**

Verse five named forgiveness and gardens; verse six names the opposite outcome for the opposite posture. It lists them one by one: the hypocrites among the men and the women, and the idolaters among the men and the women, and then the verdict — those who entertained the evil thought about God will have the evil turn on them. The punishment of God rests on them, His curse, and a Fire prepared. The two verses were put side by side so that no reader could take the promise of verse five as automatic, and so that no one could read the warning of verse six as applying only to strangers. The thought about God is the branch point, and the verse leaves it in the open with the verdict attached.
**Who the Verse Meant at Ḥudaibiyah**

The thought described here belongs to the men who sat at Ḥudaibiyah and read the treaty as a humiliation: they said among themselves that God had been overcome and His messenger abandoned. The verse answers the calculation, not the accident of speech, because the calculation was the source and the speech came after. The punishment the verse lists is not heaped on a moment of doubt; it is the outcome of deciding that God's promise needed to look like a victory on their terms.
verses.7:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**The Host in Its Kinds**

The sūrah's word for forces is the word for a host, an army, and al-Tustarī is reported to have answered the question of who the host actually is, with an answer the tafsīr tradition preserves. The host, he said, is of several kinds, and not all of it is in the sky. In the heavens the host is the prophets, and among the people of the earth it is the saints; in the heavens it is the hearts, and on the earth it is the souls. Whatever God sets in motion over a person belongs to the host, and that includes what is inside the person. A soul that God sets against its owner will bring the owner down; the bodily members, set in motion against him, do the same; a soul that takes the heart by force drags the person after mere appetite.

The sūrah states the same fact at the head of the passage, where God is said to have sent down the serenity on the believers and to have with Him the forces of the heavens and the earth (48:4 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth.”*), so that the claim is made twice around the account of the treaty. The Book's answer to the community's anxiety about its weakness is the same in both places, and it is the answer given after the battle of Ḥunayn, where a large army failed and the victory came from God (9:25–26 — *“Then Allah sent down His reassurance upon His Messenger and the believers, and sent down forces you could not see, and punished those who disbelieved.”*). The verse is not a boast about numbers; it is a statement about where the numbers come from.
verses.8:
> Indeed, ˹O Prophet,˺ We have sent you as a witness, a deliverer of good news, and a warner

**The Three Offices of the Mission**

The verse states the Prophet's mission in three nouns, and the three nouns are the offices he was sent to hold: witness, deliverer of good news, warner. The order is fixed, and the three offices divide the work of the message. The witness stands before; the deliverer of good news opens the door; the warner marks the threshold. None of the three is the mission itself, and all three together are the mission, for the message that does not witness is a report, the message that does not give glad tidings is a demand, and the message that does not warn is a rumor. The sūrah places this statement at the beginning of its second movement, immediately after the section that announced the triumph and sealed it with the ownership of the forces. The sequence is the sūrah's claim about cause and effect: the triumph is the result of the offices, and the offices are now stated so that the result can be read as what it is.

**A Witness to What and to Whom**

The first office is the one the sūrah gives first, and the exegesis divides on what it witnesses to. Another line takes the witness as the one who will bear witness for or against people in the hereafter, the testimony that stands over the outcomes, so that the office is Last-Day as well as present. The Quran gives the same triple description of the mission elsewhere, in the sūrah al-Aḥzāb, where it says, "We have sent you as a witness. A deliverer of good news, and a warner" (33:45), and the parallel fixes the formula as a standing description of the office rather than a comment on a single event.
verses.9:
> so that you ˹believers˺ may have faith in Allah and His Messenger, support and honour him, and glorify Allah morning and evening

**The Purpose of the Sending**

The verse completes the sentence of the eighth, and the completion is the purpose. The sending was not an end in itself; it was sent so that a response would occur, and the response is stated in four actions: to have faith in Allah and His Messenger, to support him, to honour him, and to glorify Allah morning and evening. The first of the four is the ground, and the other three are its fruits. Faith is the relation; support, honour, and glorification are what the relation does in the life of the person who holds it. The sūrah states the purpose in the plural of the community, the believers, and the placement of the verse at the head of the second movement fixes the purpose as the standard by which the community that follows is measured.

**The Rhythm of the Day**

The final action of the verse is the one that fixes the others in time: to glorify Allah morning and evening. The Quran places the same frame in several of its earlier addresses, in the command to remember the name morning and evening and to prostrate before it during part of the night, "Remember the Name of your Lord morning and evening. Prostrate before Him during part of the night" (76:25–26), and the range of the parallels fixes the rhythm as a standing form of the message rather than a comment on a single occasion.
verses.10:
> Surely those who pledge allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. Allah’s Hand is over theirs. Whoever breaks their pledge, it will only be to their own loss. And whoever fulfils their pledge to Allah, He will grant them a great reward

**The Pledge That Is a Pledge to God**

The verse opens with the transfer, and the transfer is its doctrine. The hand given to the one sent under the tree is, in the sūrah's statement, a hand given to the sender, and the fixing is not a figure of speech but a standing relation. The Quran states the same relation elsewhere in its plainest form, when it says that whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah (4:80 — *“Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah. But whoever turns away, then ˹know that˺ We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them”*). The logic of the two statements is identical: the one sent stands in the place of the sender, so that the act done to the one sent is done to the sending. The pledge under the tree was not a political contract between the community and its leader; it was a covenant of the community with God, held in the hand of the one God sent to hold it. The sūrah's statement of the transfer fixes the status of the event for the whole of the community's later memory, and the name the memory gave the event, the pledge of good pleasure, is the name of the transfer made into a title.

**The Hand Over the Hand**

The second sentence of the verse is the one that has occupied the commentators longest: the Hand of Allah is over their hands. The third keeps the literal sense as the sense that is true, yet holds that the actuality of the sense is unknown to the creature, because what appears of the attributes in the human order is not of the same order as the attributes themselves, and nothing is like Him (42:11 — *“There is nothing like Him, for He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing”*).

**The Covenant Remembered**

The final phrase of the verse, the pledge made to God, carries an allusion the exegesis traces to the first covenant, the one recorded in the sūrah al-Aʿrāf, when the Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify about themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They replied, "Yes, You are! We testify" (7:172). The pledge under the tree, read with the allusion, is not a new act but a reaffirmation, the community's testimony given again in the body, in the hand, in the valley outside Mecca. The sūrah links the event of Ḥudaibiyah to the first act of the human kind, and the link is the sūrah's claim about the nature of the pledge: it was always owed, and the tree was the place where it was paid. The covenant remembered is the ground on which the transfer of the first sentence stands, for a pledge to the one sent is a pledge to the sender, and the sender is the one to whom the first testimony was given before the loins.
verses.11:
> The nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, will say to you ˹O Prophet˺, “We were preoccupied with our wealth and families, so ask for forgiveness for us.” They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say, “Who then can stand between you and Allah in any way, if He intends harm or benefit for you? In fact, Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**The Question That Replaces the Answer**

The verse does not command the Prophet to argue with the excuse; it commands him to answer it with a question. Say: who then can stand between you and Allah in any way, if He intends harm or benefit for you? The question moves the ground of the debate. The excuse stands on the ground of the worldly: the wealth, the families, the fear of the Quraysh, the logistics of the stay. The question removes the ground, because the question is not about the logistics but about the ordainer, and on the ground of the ordainer the logistics are irrelevant. The exegesis gives the sense of the question: no one can avert what God desires or has ordained, and the Quran states the same sense in its plainest form elsewhere, when it says that if Allah helps, none can defeat, but if He denies help, then who else can help (3:160 — *“If Allah helps you, none can defeat you. But if He denies you help, then who else can help you? So in Allah let the believers put their trust”*). The question is the sūrah's answer, and the answer is that the excuse is addressed to the wrong court. The wealth and the families cannot stand between a person and the intention of God, and the sūrah's later verse will show what the intention of God was with the group.

**Forgiveness and Its Limits**

The group's request is the one the verse does not answer: ask for forgiveness for us. The sūrah withholds the answer here, and the answer is given elsewhere, in the sūrah that bears the name of the believers, where the limit of the Prophet's intercession is stated in the plainest terms: it is the same whether you pray for their forgiveness or not, Allah will not forgive them (63:6 — *“It is the same whether you pray for their forgiveness or not, Allah will not forgive them. Surely Allah does not guide the rebellious people”*). The two verses together state the sūrah's doctrine of the excuse. The request for forgiveness is the form the group gives its staying behind. The form is the confession, for a person who is genuinely preoccupied asks forgiveness of the preoccupation, while a person whose preoccupation is a pretext asks forgiveness of the pretext, and the asking is the admission that the pretext was known to be a pretext.

**What the Excuse Was**

The verse deals with the men of the desert who stayed behind from the journey to Makkah and afterwards offered the Prophet their property and their families as reasons, and it records the answer they were given: they had been saying that their property and their people had kept them busy, and they asked forgiveness for the community. The Book's answer is the instruction in front of us, which tells the Prophet to say that no one has any power at all over what God intends for the community. The verses that follow go further and tell the men that they thought the Messenger and the believers would never come back (48:12 — *“The truth is: you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again.”*).
**What the Answer Says About Power**

The command to answer the excuse with a question about God is one of the sūrah's sharpest statements about the limits of human arrangement. The men were presenting their circumstances as the reason they could not act, and the Book names the deeper fact that their circumstances were not outside God's disposal. The Sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān answers the men of Uḥud with the same move, telling them that they would have gone out to their deaths wherever they had been (3:154 — *“Then after distress, He sent down serenity in the form of drowsiness overcoming some of you, while others were disturbed by evil thoughts about Allah—the thoughts of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance.”*), and the Sūrah of the Spoils gives the same lesson about the decree.
**Where the Passage Goes**

The verses that follow state that the men assumed something untrue about God, and then they turn to the men who were present and give the community the promise made to them at the tree (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand”*). The sūrah's arrangement gives the excusers and the pledged side by side, and the passage in front of us is the hinge. The Book's purpose in the sūrah is to record the community's greatest test in the same chapter as its greatest promise, and the two men in front of us are the illustration.
verses.12:
> The truth is: you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again. And that was made appealing in your hearts. You harboured evil thoughts ˹about Allah˺, and ˹so˺ became a doomed people.”

**The Thought That Was Made Appealing**

The verse completes the answer the previous verse commanded, and the completion is the exposure. The truth, the sūrah says: you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again. The occasion of the thought is the event that produced the pledge, the delay of the envoy. A rumour spread that ʿUthmān had been killed, and when he did not return in time the camp took the rumour to be true, and the taking was what the pledge was made to answer. The group that stayed behind took the same rumour and drew from it the conclusion the verse names: the community would be destroyed, the Messenger would not come back, and the believers would not return.

The verse ends the diagnosis it began, and the larger passage states what the thought produced: the group that stayed behind sat and wept with grief while the community marched, and they were left to their own reasoning. The Book states the same judgement about mistaken expectations elsewhere, where the hypocrites are told that they hoped for a turn of fortune that did not come (9:52 — *“Say, “Are you awaiting anything to befall us except one of the two best things: ˹victory or martyrdom˺? But We are awaiting Allah to afflict you with torment either from Him or at our hands. So keep waiting! We too are waiting with you.”*, 57:14 — *“The tormented will cry out to those graced, “Were we not with you?” They will reply, “Yes ˹you were˺. But you chose to be tempted ˹by hypocrisy˺, ˹eagerly˺ awaited ˹our demise˺, doubted ˹the truth˺, and were deluded by false hopes until Allah’s decree ˹of your death˺ came to pass. And ˹so˺ the Chief Deceiver deceived you about Allah”*). The sūrah's interest is in the thought rather than the excuse: the men were not prevented from marching, they had already decided what God was going to do, and the verse says plainly what they thought and leaves it at that.
verses.13:
> And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, then We surely have prepared for the disbelievers a blazing Fire

**The Verdict Moves From Group to Class**

The two verses that exposed the laggards closed on the state assigned to the group, and this verse moves the judgment out of the group and into the class. The sūrah has been dealing with a specific population, the nomadic Arabs who stayed behind, and the verse widens the frame to the disbelievers as such. The movement is the sūrah's structure in action: the census of the camp is complete, and the sūrah now states the ground that stands under the camp and under every camp. The thought of the laggards, the thought that the Messenger and the believers would not return, is the seed of the thought of the disbelievers, and the first section of the sūrah had already named that thought in the hostile.

**The Blazing Fire in Its Various Names**

The word the verse gives is the bare word for the blazing fire, and the Quran carries the prepared fire under several names throughout its text. It is asserted as a humiliating punishment in the earlier sūrahs, as a painful punishment in others, and it is named together with its instruments, the chains and the shackles, in the sūrah that opens with the praise: "Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, shackles, and a blazing Fire" (76:4).
verses.14:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Sovereignty, Not Mere Force**

The sūrah's first section spoke in the vocabulary of forces, the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and this verse speaks in the vocabulary of the kingdom, and the shift of vocabulary is the shift of subject. The hosts are what the owner has at his command, the armies and the angels and the faculties of the person, and the kingdom is what the owner owns, the heavens and the earth and everything between them. The sūrah moves from the event to the ground, and the ground is stated in the form of ownership rather than in the form of power, because the event it is grounding is not a battle but a decision, the decision to forgive or to punish.

**The Two Freedoms of the Owner**

The middle sentence of the verse states the two freedoms of the owner, and the two freedoms are the verse's doctrine. The sūrah gives the formula its standing context elsewhere, in the address to the communities that spoke of themselves in the language of the chosen, where the Jews and the Christians each said, "We are the children of Allah and His most beloved," and the answer was the same formula, "He forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills. To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" (5:18).

**The Formula's Standing Form**

The formula of the verse is a standing form in the Quran, and the sūrah's use of it here fixes the form as the ground of the second section. And Allah is Most Capable of everything" (2:284), and it appears in the sūrah of the family and in the sūrah of the covenant and in the sūrah of the stars, and the range of the appearances fixes the formula as the standing ground of the Quran's own address.
verses.15:
> Those who stayed behind will say, when you ˹believers˺ set out to take the spoils of war, “Let us accompany you.” They wish to change Allah’s promise. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You will not accompany us. This is what Allah has said before.” They will then say, “In fact, you are driven by jealousy against us!” The truth is: they can hardly comprehend

**The Promise They Wish to Change**

The sūrah's charge against the return is the sentence that names the object of the wish: they wish to change the promise of Allah. The exegesis fixes the promise. The victory of Khaybar, the campaign that followed Ḥudaibiyah, was understood to have been promised to those who had been present at the pledge, in exchange for the pilgrimage they had been unable to complete. The promise was the reward of the pledge, and the reward of the pledge belongs to the pledgers, and the group's wish is to insert itself into the promise, to change its terms, to take a share of what the pledge bought. The charge is therefore not the wish to go but the wish to change, and the changing is the sin.

The verse opens the account of what the group that stayed behind will ask for, and the answer given them a verse later is that they will be told to follow an army that will fight a people of great might (48:16 — *“Say to nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, “You will be called ˹to fight˺ against a people of great might, who you will fight unless they submit.”*). The Book's interest in the spoils here is not economic but judicial: the men who sat out the campaign now want a share of the result, and the sūrah treats the request as a further instance of what they were already doing. The spoils of Khaybar function in the sūrah as a test of the same kind as the treaty was: a gift that reveals who was prepared to trust God's promise and who was not.

**The Ones Who Asked and Were Refused**

The verse names the men who had stayed behind and the request they made afterwards: they want to go out with the community when the next campaign brings spoils. The Book answers before they have spoken: they will ask, and they will be told that they will not follow, and they will be told that God had said this beforehand. The men's reply is recorded in the next verse, where they accuse the believers of envy, and the Book corrects them: no, they had understood very little. The passage is one of the sūrah's sharpest records of a group that wanted the reward of a commitment it had not made.
**The Promise the Spoils Belonged To**

The promise in the verse is the one given to the men who were present under the tree at Ḥudaybiyyah. The spoils of Khaybar were assigned to them, and the sūrah states the arrangement in its own words a few verses later, where God promised the believers great spoils that they would take, and hurried this one for them (48:20 — *“Allah has promised you ˹believers˺ abundant spoils, which you will gain, so He hastened this ˹truce˺ for you.”*). The jurists drew from the passage the rule that spoils belong to those who took part in the campaign, and the sūrah of the Spoils opens with the division of the property belonging to God and the Messenger, and to the near relatives and orphans (8:1 — *“So be mindful of Allah, settle your affairs, and obey Allah and His Messenger if you are ˹true˺ believers.”*; 8:41 — *“Know that whatever spoils you take, one-fifth is for Allah and the Messenger, his close relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers, if you ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and what We revealed to Our servant on that decisive day when the two armies met ˹at Badr˺.”*). The right follows the risk; a man who kept away from the journey had no claim on what the journey produced.
**What the Refusal Taught the Community**

The sūrah was given at a moment when the community had turned back from Makkah without entering it, and the men who had been left behind were counting on appearing for a later victory. The Book makes the assignment permanent and public, and it does so with the reason attached: the men who stayed behind had neither the hardship of the road nor the uncertainty of the encounter. The sūrah of the Spoils puts the same principle in the form of a command, telling the believers to stand firm and remember God much when they meet a force, since the help is promised to those who are present (8:45-46 — *“O believers! When you face an enemy, stand firm and remember Allah often so you may triumph”*).
verses.16:
> Say to nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, “You will be called ˹to fight˺ against a people of great might, who you will fight unless they submit. If you then obey, Allah will grant you a fine reward. But if you turn away as you did before, He will inflict upon you a painful punishment.”

**The People of Great Might**

The exegesis divides on the identity of the people of great might, and the three lines of the division are worth weighing. One line takes them as the tribe of the Ḥanīfa, the community that the armies of the first caliph, Abū Bakr, defeated in the years after the Prophet's death. Another takes the verse as pointing ahead to the future wars against the two great empires, Byzantium and Persia, the powers that would come against the Muslim state. A third takes them as the tribes of the Hawāzin and the Thaqīf, the confederacy that met the Muslim army in the field after the conquest of Makkah.

The second line of reading looks past Arabia to the two great powers of the age: the Persian empire to the east and the Byzantine empire to the north, the armies the community would meet in the campaigns of the following years. The sūrah pairs the command with a condition — fight until they submit or accept Islam — and with the alternative for those who turn away: a painful punishment. The point of the passage is that the test of the treaty is followed by a harder test, and the same men who failed the first one are offered a second chance with its terms stated in full.

---

**The Call and the Two Conditions**

The verse gives the terms in full. The men who stayed behind would be called, then they would face one of two conditions: *you will fight them, or they will submit* — so that the test is stated in advance and nothing is left to surprise. If they answer, the reward from God is named as good, with no mention of spoils taken from these particular enemies; if they turn their backs as they did before, the painful punishment stands. The Arabic of *yuslimūn* carries both a military sense of surrender and the religious sense of entering the faith, and the commentators left the second open. The passage reads as mercy for men who had failed the first test: a second door, with everything written on it.
verses.17:
> There is no blame on the blind, or the disabled, or the sick ˹for staying behind˺. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted by Him into Gardens under which rivers flow. But whoever turns away will be subjected by Him to a painful punishment

**The Parallel Verse and Its Frame**

The Quran gives the exemption in its full form elsewhere, in the sūrah that closes the revelation, where the parallel is stated with its condition and its fourth category: "There is no blame on the weak, the sick, or those lacking the means ˹if they stay behind˺, as long as they are true to Allah and His Messenger. There is no blame on the good-doers. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (9:91). The parallel adds to the sūrah's list the fourth category, those lacking the means, the poverty that is the ground of the stay as the blindness is the ground of it. It adds the condition, the truth to Allah and His Messenger, which fixes the exemption on the heart rather than on the body alone. The two verses together state the teaching about the exemption in its full form. The sūrah's verse gives the exemption in its bare form, the three categories and the no blame, and the parallel gives it in its full form, the four categories and the condition. The bare form is the sūrah's way of stating the principle, and the full form is the Quran's way of stating the application, and the application is the principle in its details.

**The Obedience That Admits**

The verse's second sentence states the pair in its plainest form, and the plainness is the sūrah's move. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, the one who has the ground of the going and takes it, is admitted by Him into the Gardens under which rivers flow, and the admission is the Gardens. The Quran states the stark contrast of the obedience and the turning away throughout its text. The sūrah of the light gives it in the form the sūrah's verse takes: the obedience to God and to the Messenger is the obedience that carries the person to the right guidance. The messenger is accountable only for the burden with which he was charged, while each of the people is accountable for the burden with which they were charged (24:54 — *“Say, “Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.”*).
verses.18:
> Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand

**The Tree and the Number**

The sūrah does not name the tree, and the tradition that preserves the event names it. The tree under which the pledge was made was a samurah, an acacia, the tafsīr tradition reports, and the naming is the community's way of making the verse concrete. The number of the pledgers is reported in two figures, the one over thirteen hundred, the other about fifteen hundred, and the two figures are the range of the community's own count. The form of the pledge is reported in two readings. The two readings are the range of the community's own memory: the majority of the accounts take the pledge as the pledge that they would not flee. Some take it as the pledge that they would fight the Quraysh until death, and the two readings are not opposed, because a pledge that is not to flee is, in the situation, the pledge to fight.

---

The pledge under the tree was the pledge of Ridwān, and the reports describe it in full: the Prophet ﷺ called for allegiance from the men who had come with him to ʿUmrah after word spread that ʿUthmān had been killed at Makkah, and they pledged to stand firm without leaving the field. The number is given in the sūrah's next verse as well, and the reports in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections count them around fourteen hundred. The knowledge God had of what was in their hearts is the promise attached to the pledge: tranquillity sent down and the reward of a near victory, which the sūrah states in the same verse. The tree was remembered afterwards, and the Companions' practice reflects the honour of the event rather than veneration of the tree, which the reports say the Prophet ﷺ declined.
verses.19:
> and many spoils of war they will gain. For Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**The Spoils of the Near Campaign**

The exegesis fixes the spoils in their first reference, and the first reference is the campaign that followed the treaty. The abundant spoils, on the sūrah's own account, are the spoils of Khaybar, the fortified oasis to the north of Madinah, and the campaign for it was the first campaign the community engaged in after the departure from Ḥudaibiyah. The spoils promised to the pledgers at the tree were paid at Khaybar, and the payment is the sūrah's way of making the promise history. The exegesis notes the sequence of the events: the departure from the valley, the return to Medina, and then the march for the oasis, and the sequence is the sūrah's way of saying that the payment followed the promise without a gap.

The sūrah places these spoils after the pledge under the tree, where God's good pleasure was announced and the serenity came down (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand”*), so that the gift follows the obedience in the order of the text as well as in the order of events. The Book states the same principle in Sūrah al-Ḥashr, where the property taken from the disbelievers is called a spoils granted by God (59:6–7 — *“As for the gains Allah has turned over to His Messenger from them—you did not ˹even˺ spur on any horse or camel for such gains. But Allah gives authority to His messengers over whoever He wills. For Allah is Most Capable of everything”*), and it names Khaybar in the account of what the Messenger was given after the treaty. The community's share is stated as a fact rather than a reward, and the next verse adds what is still to come.
verses.20:
> Allah has promised you ˹believers˺ abundant spoils, which you will gain, so He hastened this ˹truce˺ for you. And He has held people’s hands back from ˹harming˺ you, so it may be a sign for the believers, and so He may guide you along the Straight Path

**The Promise Stated Twice**

The spoils are promised again, and the second promise is the sūrah's way of saying that the spoils are the center of its second half. The previous verse stated the spoils as the second half of the reward of the pledge, and this verse states them as a promise in their own right, a promise made to the believers as a community. The exegesis gives the relation of the two mentions in its two lines: the second is a reiteration of the first to emphasis, or it is a reference to greater spoils beyond those named in the previous verse. The two lines are the sūrah's way of saying that the repetition is not a redundancy, and that the center of the sūrah's second half is the statement of the reward. The three verses of the reward, from the spoils they will gain to the gains beyond the reach, form the sūrah's census of the promise, and the census is the sūrah's claim about the treaty.

**The Spoils Promised and the Spoils Given**

The verse is addressed to the men who had stood by the treaty at Ḥudaybiyyah. God promises them plenty of spoils in the future, and says that this one was hurried for them. The reference is to Khaybar, whose property was given to the men who had been at Ḥudaybiyyah and who had not been able to accompany the Prophet on an earlier expedition. The community had felt the treaty as a loss, since they had come to Makkah expecting to make the pilgrimage and turned back, and the verse says that the recompense came quickly and that what was waiting was more.
**The Hands That Were Held Back**

The second clause is about protection rather than property: God held the hands of the people back from you. The men at Ḥudaybiyyah were unarmed pilgrims, in the territory of their enemies, and they came home safely. The Book reads that safety as an act of God with a purpose attached: so that it may be a sign for the believers. The same word is used in the verse after this one, where the spoils the community could not yet reach are described as already in God's hand (48:21 — *“And ˹there are˺ other gains which are beyond your reach that Allah is keeping in store ˹for you˺. For Allah is Most Capable of everything”*). The passage is about the difference between what a person can see and what has been arranged, and it teaches the community that a treaty that looked like a defeat was itself the gift.
**Why the Verse Matters to the Sūrah**

The sūrah of Victory opens with the treaty and calls it a clear victory. This verse explains the economics of that sentence: a promise of future gain, a quick gain in the present, and protection that nobody in the community had planned. The Book is showing the men who had just been turned away from the House that the same hand that stopped them at the gate had already arranged what came next, and the closing words, that God may guide you to a straight path, tie the whole arrangement to guidance rather than to booty.
verses.21:
> And ˹there are˺ other gains which are beyond your reach that Allah is keeping in store ˹for you˺. For Allah is Most Capable of everything

**The Gains Beyond the Reach**

The verse is the third statement of the reward, and the third statement is the sūrah's way of extending the promise beyond the horizon of the event. Other gains, the verse says, and the other is the word that carries the extension. The gains are other than the spoils named in the two previous verses, and they are beyond the reach of the community at the moment the verse is stated. The exegesis gives the reference in its lines: further spoils of war beyond the spoils of the near campaign, the gains of the oasis to the north, the conquest of the city of the house, the future wars against the two empires of Persia and Byzantium, the whole range of the openings that would come to the Muslim community, or the rewards of the inner order.

The commentators read these other gains as the conquest of Mecca, which came two years after the treaty and which gives the sūrah its name, and they note that the verse says they were not yet able to achieve them. The Book states the same promise in this sūrah's opening verses, where the near victory and the greater victory are distinguished (48:1 — *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”*, 48:27 — *“Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger’s vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security—˹some with˺ heads shaved and ˹others with˺ hair shortened—without fear. He knew what you did not know, so He first granted you the triumph at hand”*), so that the reader sees the treaty and the conquest as one event in two stages. The phrase that God has encompassed them completes the thought: the outcome does not depend on the resources of the community but on the decree of the One who promised it.
verses.22:
> If the disbelievers were to fight you, they would certainly flee. Then they would never find any protector or helper

**The Flight and the Absence of the Helper**

The verse states the two outcomes of the counterfactual in their order, the flight and the absence of the helper, and the order is the sūrah's way of stating the end of the one who fights and loses. They would have turned their backs, and then they would have found neither protector nor helper, and the then is the sūrah's way of fixing the sequence. The exegesis gives the range of the absence: it refers to the situation in this life and in the next. The Quran states the formula elsewhere in its standing form, in the sūrah of the women, where the proud and the arrogant are the ones who find no helper, "And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper" (4:173). The sūrah's verse takes the standing formula and applies it to the counterfactual, and the application is the sūrah's way of saying that the end of the hostile is the end the Quran has already named. The absence of the helper is the sūrah's name for the state of the one whose power has gone, and the state is what the counterfactual reaches.
verses.23:
> ˹This is˺ Allah’s way, already long established ˹in the past˺. And you will find no change in Allah’s way

**A Standing Pattern, Named**

The verse names the pattern, and the name is the word for the wont, the way, the standing form of the dealings of God with the communities he addresses. The sūrah states the event of Ḥudaibiyah as an instance of the wont, and the stating is the sūrah's way of saying that the event is not an exception. The exegesis fixes the reference in its usual line: the wont here is the way God deals with those who fight his prophets, and the Quran states the wont in its plainest form in the sūrah of the divorce, where the declaration is that God and his messengers will surely prevail. The sūrah's verse takes the wont and applies it to the event, and the application is the sūrah's claim. The event at Ḥudaibiyah, the turning back and the treaty and the held-back hands, is the wont made visible in the community's own history, and the visibility is what the sūrah's naming gives it.

**The Pattern Stated in the Past**

The verse states the wont in the past, and the past is the sūrah's way of saying that the pattern is not a new thing. The way of Allah, already long established, the verse says, and the establishment is in the communities that came before. The Quran states the wont in its earlier addresses, in the sūrah of the fleet, where the formula of the no-change is given in its standing form: "You will find no change in the way of Allah, nor will you find it diverted" (35:43). The sūrah's verse takes the formula and states it in the form of the event, and the form is the sūrah's way of saying that the event is the wont made present.
verses.24:
> He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**The Double Holding Back**

The verse states the holding back in its full form, and the full form is the double act. He held back their hands from you, and your hands from them, and the doubling is the sūrah's way of saying that the peace was not the result of one side's restraint. The hands of the Quraysh were held back from the Muslims, and the hands of the Muslims were held back from the Quraysh, and the two holdings are the work of the one who holds both. The sūrah's statement of the double is its way of saying that the treaty was not a concession made by the weaker side to the stronger, and that the restraint was not the absence of the power to fight. The double holding is the sūrah's name for the peace, and the name is the sūrah's claim about the event.

**The Upper Hand That Was Given**

The verse states the holding back after the giving of the upper hand, and the sequence is the sūrah's way of fixing the ground of the restraint. After having made you victorious over them, the verse says, and the victory over them is the upper hand that the Muslims held before the hands were held back. The exegesis gives the reference of the upper hand in its account of the event, and the account is the group that tried the surprise attack before the treaty was ratified. The Muslims had the upper hand over that group, and the upper hand is the sūrah's way of saying that the holding back was not the result of the Muslims' weakness. The restraint was made on the ground of the strength, and the ground is what the sūrah's sequence states.
verses.25:
> They are the ones who persisted in disbelief and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque, preventing the sacrificial animals from reaching their destination. ˹We would have let you march through Mecca,˺ had there not been believing men and women, unknown to you. You might have trampled them underfoot, incurring guilt for ˹what you did to˺ them unknowingly. That was so Allah may admit into His mercy whoever He wills. Had those ˹unknown˺ believers stood apart, We would have certainly inflicted a painful punishment on the disbelievers

**The House They Were Kept From**

The verse names what the community lost that week: the men who rejected the message held them back from the Sacred House, and they stopped the sacrificial animals from reaching the place where they were to be offered. The pilgrimage had been prepared and begun, and it ended at the border. The Book treats being kept away from the Sacred House as a major offence and it names it in several sūrahs, so the verse records it as one of the wrongs of the men of Makkah and not as an accident of travel. The Book also explains why the standoff ended without a battle: there were believing men and believing women in the city whose faith was not known to anybody, and if the community had marched in, those believers would have been killed by their own brothers in faith without anybody knowing. The verse says that this is the reason the fighting did not happen, and it says that God willed to admit into His mercy whom He liked and that He would have punished the rejecters if the two groups had been separated.

**Why the Two Sides Did Not Meet**

The mercy in the arrangement was inside the enemy city: hidden believers mixed into the population that the army would have attacked. The Book says that if they had been a separate group, the believers would have been allowed to fight and punish the men of Makkah who rejected the message, but the two could not be told apart. The teachers of the community drew from this a general rule: the safety of the believers who cannot be distinguished from the enemy is a reason to hold back from an attack, because the community may not buy a victory with the blood of its own people. The verse in front of the reader states the rule in the middle of an account of a treaty that the men of the community found hard to accept.

**The Treaty That Looked Like a Loss**

The chapter names the treaty a clear victory at its opening (48:1 states it — *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”*), which told the community to look at the week from a different angle than the one they were looking from. The verses that follow the treaty describe the pledges that were made under the tree and the calm that came down on the believers (48:18 records the pledge — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree.”*), and the sūrah promises that they will enter the Sacred House safely with their heads shaved and their hair cut short (48:27 states the promise — *“Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger’s vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security—˹some with˺ heads shaved and ˹others with˺ hair shortened—without fear.”*). The verse in front of the reader holds the moment when none of that was visible: the road was closed, the animals were stopped, the men were angry, and the believers inside the city were in danger. The chapter's lesson is the one it draws at the close of the account: the matter that God had already decided was working itself out through the events that looked like a defeat.

**What the Verse Records for the Community**

The verse keeps the memory of the men and women who could not be seen and could not be helped, and it keeps the memory of the wrong done to the community on the road. Both are needed: the first tells the community that God knows the believers it cannot see, and the second tells it what kind of power it was dealing with. The sūrah also says that God knows what a person carries inside him, and it names the pledge that the community gave in that same journey (48:10 — *“Allah’s Hand is over theirs.”* states that the hand of God was over their hands, and 48:24 — *“He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”* describes the encounter that was prevented). The verse in front of the reader is the account of a pilgrimage that did not reach its goal and a mercy that arrived through the door nobody expected.
verses.26:
> ˹Remember˺ when the disbelievers had filled their hearts with pride—the pride of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance—then Allah sent down His serenity upon His Messenger and the believers, inspiring them to uphold the declaration of faith, for they were better entitled and more worthy of it. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**The Third Descent of the Serenity**

The verse is the sūrah's third sending of the serenity, and the sending is upon the Messenger and upon the believers, and the double object is the sūrah's way of stating that the serenity reached the leader and the community together. The context of the third descent is the whole week accumulated: the turning back from the house, the delay of the envoy, the terms of the treaty that some resented, the command that met the sitting, the refusal of the people of Makkah to allow the names at the head of the document. The serenity, in the sūrah's account, is the descent that meets the accumulation, and the meeting is the sūrah's way of stating that the state of the believers at the close of the week was the state of the held.

The serenity is sent down three times in the sūrah — with the vow in 48:4 — *“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith.”*, at the pledge of 48:18 — *“He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand”*, and here at the moment of the standoff — and that repetition is how the sūrah structures the whole event. This verse also states what God required in exchange for keeping the community from fighting: the word of *taqwā*, the word of God-consciousness, which the commentators read as the declaration of God's oneness and which the Prophet is said to have identified as *lā ilāha illā Allāh*. The sūrah places the people of the treaty on two levels in one verse: the pride that held the Meccans in place, and the restraint that God placed in the hearts of the believers, who were made worthy of it.

**What the Verse Names**

The verse says that God sent down His serenity upon the Messenger and upon the believers and bound them to the word of mindfulness, since they were the people of it and entitled to it, and it says that the disbelievers had put in their hearts the fervour of the age of ignorance. The passage is the sūrah's account of the treaty at Ḥudaybiyyah, and the word of mindfulness is read as the phrase the men recited as the pledge, the declaration of God's oneness. The Book contrasts the two dispositions: a hot temper in one camp and a settled word in the other.
**What the Treaty Was**

The reports describe the day the Quraysh sent a delegation and the terms were written down, and the one clause that the community objected to was the mention of the Prophet's title. The verse before this one describes the men who sent their tranquillity away and the men who received it, and the sūrah's opening calls the treaty a clear victory (48:1 — *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”*). The Book's account of the treaty names the restraint as the thing that made it a victory, and the verse in front of us states where the restraint came from.
**The Serenity in the Sūrah**

The sūrah mentions the serenity three times, and the three sendings happen at the three points of the story: at the flight from Makkah (48:4 — *“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith. To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise”*), at the treaty itself (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand”*), and here at the refusal of the Quraysh to let the community enter (48:26 — *“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things”*). The Book's word for it describes a quietness that settles on a person's chest in the middle of a public crisis, and the sūrah gives the community the same medicine at each stage. The verse in front of us is the last of the three, and the sūrah places it before the account of the vision being fulfilled.
verses.27:
> Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger’s vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security—˹some with˺ heads shaved and ˹others with˺ hair shortened—without fear. He knew what you did not know, so He first granted you the triumph at hand

**The Vision That Made the Journey**

The verse states the fulfillment in its first clause, and the first clause is the sūrah's way of closing the account of the journey. God has fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth, the verse says, and the fulfilling is the sūrah's way of stating that the journey had its ground in the vision. The exegesis gives the vision in its form: in the dream the Prophet saw himself and his people making their way into the city and going round the house. He spoke of the dream to the community in the houses of Medina, before a single pilgrim had mounted, and the speaking is the ground on which the journey was made.

The vision is the dream in which the Prophet saw himself and his companions entering the Sacred Mosque, heads shaved and hair trimmed, and the Book reports the fulfilment as a fact before it happened. The commentators tie the completion to the conquest of Mecca in the eighth year, and they note the clause in the same verse that guards the promise: God knew what the community did not know, and He gave them a conquest near at hand, which is the treaty itself. So one verse holds the dream, its delay, and its fulfilment, and it is the sūrah's own summary of how the promise given at Ḥudaybiyah came true.

**What the Vision Was**

The verse states that God has fulfilled the vision of His Messenger in truth, that the community would enter the Sacred Mosque in safety with their heads shaved or their hair cut short and without fear. The reports place the vision before the treaty at Ḥudaybiyyah, when the Prophet told the companions what he had seen and they understood that they were going to make the pilgrimage that year. The sūrah then records the treaty and the disappointment, and this verse is placed after the account of the men who stayed behind and the spoils of Khaybar, so that the fulfilment is stated before the door opens.
**What the Verse Adds to the Vision**

The verse adds two things the earlier account had not stated: that the entry would be in safety, and that God knew what the community did not know, and so He gave them a victory close at hand. The reports name the victory as the treaty itself, and the sūrah's own opening calls it a clear victory (48:1 — *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”*). The Book's arrangement tells the reader that the vision and the treaty were the same promise seen from two angles, and the following year's pilgrimage delivered it.
**Where the Passage Is Standing**

The verses around it deal with the men who came with the Prophet to the tree and gave their pledge, and the sūrah names God's pleasure with them and the calm that came down on them (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree.”*). The verse in front of us gathers the whole account into the sentence that the vision was true, and the community's own history recorded what followed: the entry into Makkah in safety within the year, in the manner the verse describes.
verses.28:
> He is the One Who has sent His Messenger with ˹right˺ guidance and the religion of truth, making it prevail over all others. And sufficient is Allah as a Witness

**The Sending Stated in Its Final Form**

The sūrah now states the sending in its final form, and the form is the ground of everything the sūrah has stated. He sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, the verse says, and the sending is the sūrah's way of placing the event on its first ground. The movement of the sūrah has carried the reader from the announcement of the triumph to the account of the pledge and the plea and the serenity and the spoils and the vision. The verse now states the ground under the movement: the event was the event of the sent one, and the sent one was sent with the guidance and the religion.

The Book repeats this verse almost word for word in Sūrah al-Tawbah and Sūrah al-Ṣaff (9:33 — *“He is the One Who has sent His Messenger with ˹true˺ guidance and the religion of truth, making it prevail over all others, even to the dismay of the polytheists”*; 61:9 — *“He is the One Who has sent His Messenger with ˹true˺ guidance and the religion of truth, making it prevail over all others, even to the dismay of the polytheists”*), and the three occurrences are one declaration of the destination of the message. The verse ends with a sentence that restates the claim in terms of witness: God is sufficient as a witness, so the argument does not depend on the community's standing or on any human endorsement. The place of the verse in the sūrah is deliberate: the treaty that looked like a defeat is followed by a sentence about a religion that will prevail, and the reader is left to hold the two together.

---

**What the Words Had to Survive**

A promise of this size — a religion that will prevail over every other — has to survive two tests that no one at Ḥudaibiyah would have passed in advance: the test of the treaty itself, and the test of history. The first was answered in the same decade, when the community returned and the city that had barred them opened, and when the message went out from Madinah in letters to the rulers of Byzantium and Persia. The second answer took a generation: within a century the call was being heard from the western edge of the known world to the borders of China, among peoples who had never heard the word Ḥudaibiyah. None of that is offered as the proof of the verse, since the verse rests on God's own witness. It is simply what the promise looked like when time arrived, and the men who signed the document were the first witnesses of it.
**The Witness Named**

The verse ends with *God is sufficient as a witness* — no assembly, no notary, no ratification by the powerful. The claim does not need the community's standing to hold. Only God's knowledge is called to attest that the Messenger was sent with the guidance and the religion of truth, which is why the claim could be made in a year when the community could not hold a road to their own sanctuary.
verses.29:
> Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. And those with him are firm with the disbelievers and compassionate with one another. You see them bowing and prostrating ˹in prayer˺, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure. The sign ˹of brightness can be seen˺ on their faces from the trace of prostrating ˹in prayer˺. This is their description in the Torah. And their parable in the Gospel is that of a seed that sprouts its ˹tiny˺ branches, making it strong. Then it becomes thick, standing firmly on its stem, to the delight of the planters—in this way Allah makes the believers a source of dismay for the disbelievers. To those of them who believe and do good, Allah has promised forgiveness and a great reward

**The Two Faces**

*Muḥammadun rasūlu Allāh* — Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and the sentence stands as a heading for what follows. Then the verse gives the community that is with him two faces: hard on the disbelievers, and merciful among themselves. The two belong together, and the Book does not let either be dropped. A community that is only hard becomes a gang, and a community that is only soft loses its purpose; the verse states both in one line and leaves the reader to see that the severity outside and the mercy inside are what make the group hold together. The Sūrah of the Table gives the same picture in other words, promising that God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, gentle with the believers and firm with the disbelievers (5:54 — *“O believers! Whoever among you abandons their faith, Allah will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him.”*).
**The Mark on the Faces**

The verse describes them as bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and His pleasure, and it says their mark is on their faces from the trace of the prostration. The commentators read the mark in two ways: a visible change in the face that comes from long worship, or, more precisely, the humility and light that people see in a person who prays. The Book does not say the mark is a brand on the skin; it says the trace of prostration, and the two readings leave the reader with the same thing to look for.
**The Two Books and the Plant**

Then the verse states that this is their description in the Torah, and that their description in the Gospel is a plant that puts out its shoot, is strengthened by it, becomes thick, and stands firm on its stalk, pleasing the farmers — and the purpose in both places is that the disbelievers may be enraged by them. The image is the picture of a community growing from weakness into a body with a spine, which is exactly what the first decade of Madinah looked like. The commentators noted the correspondence with the parables of seed and growth in the Gospel, and the verse uses the picture to say what the community is for: a thing that stands and cannot be pulled up, and that angers the people who had expected it to wilt.
**The Promise**

The verse closes with the promise: God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward. Every description in the sentence — the severity, the mercy, the worship, the growth — is gathered under those two words, belief and good work. The sūrah of Victory has just described the treaty that looked like a defeat, and this verse is its closing portrait of the community that had signed it. The Book's answer to a hard year is not a promise of ease; it is a picture of what the community becomes. The verse names the Prophet and his companions as the description found in the earlier books, and the companions themselves were the proof of the description: the marks on their faces came from the long prostration, and the reports describe the dust on their foreheads from the places of prayer. The sūrah closes on this picture because the treaty it has just described looked like a defeat to the men who signed it, and the closing verse answers them with what the community becomes rather than with what it won that week. The Book says the same about the men who were with the Prophet when it tells the believers that God was pleased with them under the tree (48:18 — *“Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree.”* states the pledge and the calm that came with it), and the verse before the reader gathers the whole community into two sentences: hard on the enemy of God, gentle among themselves, and steady in prayer.
